nodes.content: Develop continual visual recognition that distinguishes novel classes from recurring appearance shifts without task boundaries or stored images.
requirements: Achieve novelty-detection AUROC ≥0.90 when unseen classes and recurring appearance shifts coexist.
Limit mean old-class accuracy decline from post-acquisition performance to ≤5 percentage points.

nodes.content: Maintain online class-by-appearance feature prototypes; detect novelty via shift-marginalized class likelihoods and rehearse adapters on prototypes without storing images.
Which prototype score distinguishes a returning camera style from a new class when each known class spans multiple styles?
Maximum classwise style-marginalized Mahalanobis likelihood will achieve novelty AUROC ≥0.90, outperforming nearest-prototype distance on recurring shifts.
Run boundary-free DomainNet streams with recurring domains and held-out classes; compare novelty AUROC for classwise marginal likelihood versus nearest-prototype distance.
On boundary-free DomainNet, style-marginalized likelihood achieved 0.93 novelty AUROC versus 0.84 for nearest-prototype distance.
Adopt style-marginalized likelihood for novelty scoring because its DomainNet AUROC exceeded nearest-prototype distance by 0.09.
With the selected likelihood scorer fixed, tune prototype-only adapter rehearsal; validate DomainNet novelty AUROC and old-class accuracy decline.
Sweep prototype-only adapter rehearsal weights {0, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0} on boundary-free DomainNet; measure novelty AUROC and post-acquisition old-class accuracy decline.
DomainNet rehearsal-sweep report with per-weight novelty AUROC, old-class accuracy decline, and three-seed confidence intervals.
At 90% unseen-class TPR, recurring-domain false-positive rate was 12% for marginal likelihood versus 29% for nearest-prototype distance.
Nearest-prototype distance alone keeps recurring-domain false positives below 15% at 90% unseen-class TPR on boundary-free DomainNet.
Select a rehearsal weight meeting ≤5-point decline from the DomainNet sweep report, then retest nearest-prototype recurring-domain FPR at 90% TPR.
With 0.5-weight rehearsal, nearest-prototype recurring-domain FPR remained 24% at 90% unseen-class TPR; old-class accuracy declined 4.2 points.
Given nearest-prototype's 24% false-positive rate, pair marginal likelihood with 0.5-weight rehearsal; measure novelty AUROC and old-class accuracy decline.
Evaluate marginal-likelihood scoring with 0.5-weight prototype rehearsal on three-seed boundary-free DomainNet; record novelty AUROC and post-acquisition old-class decline.
Three-seed DomainNet joint-evaluation table reporting marginal-likelihood novelty AUROC and mean post-acquisition old-class accuracy decline under 0.5-weight rehearsal.
Audit joint-evaluation table against both thresholds; analyze recurring-domain false positives at 90% unseen-class TPR to assess shift-versus-novelty discrimination.
Learn a shared online appearance subspace; detect novelty from orthogonal class residuals and preserve old weights using Fisher regularization.
Can an online appearance subspace remove recurring-domain variation without projecting away features that distinguish unseen classes?
Removing the top four within-class appearance directions yields novelty AUROC ≥0.90 on boundary-free DomainNet without erasing unseen-class separation.
Using the rehearsal-sweep report, fix 0.5-weight rehearsal; compare zero versus four removed directions on DomainNet novelty AUROC and unseen-class margins.
On DomainNet, four-direction removal raised novelty AUROC from 0.86 to 0.91; unseen-class cosine separation remained 0.38 versus 0.39.
Apply four-direction removal with 0.5-weight rehearsal selected from the sweep; test novelty AUROC and unseen-class margins on rare-domain DomainNet streams.
On boundary-free DomainNet rare-domain streams, four-direction removal cut unseen-class separation from 0.39 to 0.18; novelty AUROC reached 0.84.
Replace fixed four-direction removal with adaptive rank, rejecting directions that reduce unlabeled cluster separation >10%; predict rare-domain novelty AUROC ≥0.90.
Calibrate adaptive-rank gating using standard-domain 0.38 separation and rare-domain 0.18 collapse; test rare-domain AUROC with sweep-selected 0.5 rehearsal.
Adaptive-rank gating restored rare-domain unseen-class separation to 0.35 and raised novelty AUROC from 0.84 to 0.91.
Select adaptive-rank gating: fixed removal improved standard DomainNet but failed rare domains; gating restored rare-domain novelty AUROC to 0.91.
With adaptive-rank gating selected, tune image-free Fisher regularization; verify rare-domain novelty AUROC ≥0.90 and old-class decline ≤5 points.
Sweep Fisher penalties {0, 0.1, 1, 10} with adaptive-rank gating on rare-domain DomainNet; measure novelty AUROC and old-class decline.
Rare-domain DomainNet Fisher-sweep table listing each penalty’s novelty AUROC, post-acquisition old-class accuracy decline, and three-seed intervals.
Use a sticky hidden Markov model to track returning appearance regimes with regime-conditioned conformal novelty scores and frozen-backbone class heads.
How can regime-conditioned conformal scores distinguish new classes from returning appearance regimes without contaminating online calibration?
Updating regime-specific conformal quantiles only when HMM regime posterior exceeds 0.95 and class confidence exceeds 0.90 preserves novelty AUROC ≥0.90.
Use the Fisher-sweep table to select a retention-safe comparator; compare 0.95/0.90-gated versus ungated HMM calibration using DomainNet novelty AUROC.
On DomainNet recurring-regime streams, gated calibration achieved 0.92 novelty AUROC versus 0.85 ungated; calibration contamination fell from 14% to 3%.
Using the Fisher-sweep table for retention-matched comparison, stress-test gated calibration on 20-frame DomainNet regime returns; measure novelty AUROC and contamination.
On 20-frame DomainNet regime returns, gated calibration fell to 0.86 novelty AUROC, with 9% calibration contamination.
Freeze quantile updates for 32 frames after regime returns and reuse prior calibration sketches; predict 20-frame-return novelty AUROC ≥0.90.
Use Fisher-sweep retention matching; compare 32-frame sketch freezes with the 0.86-AUROC gated baseline on 20-frame returns, tracking contamination against 3%.
On 20-frame returns, sketch freezing raised novelty AUROC from 0.86 to 0.91 and reduced calibration contamination from 9% to 2%.
Adopt 32-frame calibration freezes: gating worked on ordinary returns but failed rapid returns; freezing restored AUROC to 0.91.
With 32-frame freezes adopted, test frozen-backbone heads on rapid-return streams for novelty AUROC ≥0.90 and old-class decline ≤5 points.
Select retention-matched Fisher comparator from sweep; test 32-frame freezes with frozen-backbone heads on rapid-return DomainNet, recording AUROC and old-class decline.
Rapid-return DomainNet comparison table with novelty AUROC, old-class accuracy decline, and retention-matched Fisher-baseline metrics across three seeds.
Audit table against AUROC ≥0.90 and decline ≤5 points; compare ordinary (3%), rapid-return (9%), and frozen-sketch (2%) contamination.
Rapid-return DomainNet audit found 0.91 novelty AUROC, 3.8-point old-class decline, and 2% calibration contamination under frozen-sketch HMM.
Retain frozen-sketch HMM for rapid returns: its 0.91 AUROC and 3.8-point decline meet both goals after adopting calibration freezes.
